Chapter 34

An adapter, from scratch

What an adapter is: writeClient, writePrerendered, generateServerInstance per function, a runtime bundled with rolldown, an instrumentation initializer and builder.instrument, an emulate() for development, and adapter-provided Vite plugins. Then the part that is only this adapter: a catch-all with no routes, and applyReroute.

By the end of this chapter

Read a whole adapter and know which five steps every adapter takes; understand the server-per-function split; and see how SvelteKit 3’s applyReroute hands a request between functions.

An adapter is the thing that takes SvelteKit’s build output and turns it into a program for a particular place. Everything up to step 2 in that list is *every* adapter; everything after it is this one. It targets a plain Node process, like adapter-node, and is smaller in every way that does not matter and one that does: it deploys the app as two functions and a catch-all.

The split, and a manifest per function

Why split at all

A single function would be simpler and, for this app, faster. But a single function never *needs* applyReroute, and the reason SvelteKit 3 added it is precisely that platforms split apps across functions. An adapter that shows how the hand-off works has to split something, and /api is the natural seam: the part somebody would scale, cache and rate-limit differently. Fully prerendered routes go to neither — they are files.

builder.generateServerInstance(dest, { routes }) writes a module whose server knows *only* those routes. Three are written: pages, api, and one with no routes at all. It replaced generateManifest in 3.0, and the difference is what the adapter gets to see: a manifest string to pair with a Server class before, nothing now — the manifest’s shape is SvelteKit’s business, SSRManifest is no longer a public type, and an adapter that read it would break on the next change. A server with no routes can still run the hooks — and when reroute changes the path of a request it received, SvelteKit sets an x-sveltekit-rerouted-url header on the response. That header is set only when the route table is empty, which is why the catch-all is route-less rather than a copy of pages. entries.js carries what the runtime needs that only the build knows: the origin baked in for CSRF, the prerendered paths, the route patterns as regex sources.

Bundling the runtime

Four bundles, not one. SvelteKit 3 configures a server as *module-level* state — server.init writes the manifest into the runtime that server.respond reads — so one module graph holds exactly one server, and three in one bundle means the last init wins and every route answers 404. Each function is therefore bundled on its own under functions/, with its own copy of the app, and the runtime in files/ is bundled once more beside them. The runtime does not import the functions at all: handler.js loads functions/<name>/index.js by path when the process starts, and the names travel through entries.js. Production dependencies stay external and everything else is bundled in, so build/ runs with pnpm install --prod. One thing must not be bundled twice: the OpenTelemetry API, or the SvelteKit runtime and the instrumentation file would report spans to two different worlds. And one thing must be bundled *with* the server rather than beside it: the instrumentation initializer from createInstrumentationInitializer, which fills in the environment before instrumentation.server.js runs and has to share the server’s copy of env.js to do it — hence the extra entry.

builder.instrument renames index.js to start.js and writes a new index.js that imports the initializer, then the instrumentation file, and *then* dynamically imports start.js. That order is the whole feature (ch. 32): the environment exists before the SDK asks for it, and the SDK is registered before the modules it patches are loaded.

Three more things an adapter can declare. emulate() fills in event.platform during vite dev, vite build and vite preview, with the same shape the runtime produces, so nothing has to guard against undefined. supports says what the runtime can do — read() from $app/server, instrumentation. And in SvelteKit 3 an adapter can contribute Vite plugins, pre or post: this one provides virtual:adapter, which the diagnostics page imports.

The two comments disagree. The type’s says emulate() fills in event.platform during vite dev and vite preview; the adapter’s, above it, says vite dev, vite build and vite preview. The adapter’s is right, and the SvelteKit docs on writing adapters agree: the build prerenders the landing page, and a prerendered page gets its event.platform from emulate() as well. The type’s comment is simply older than the prerendering.

The runtime: four steps per request

Three servers, each written by generateServerInstance — the whole SvelteKit runtime each, init and respond and nothing else, with a different idea of which routes exist, each in a bundle of its own. 3.0 deprecated the Server class for these ready-made objects: an adapter no longer builds a server from a manifest, it imports one. It imports them *by path*, with a dynamic import() computed from dir.js, and the comment says why the obvious alternative failed: three static imports rewritten by rolldown into ./functions/… land in whatever chunk the bundler put this code in — index.js and handler.js are both entries, so their shared body became chunks/handler-….js — and from there the relative path points at nothing. The end-to-end suite found that one on its first run against the new adapter. server.init runs the app’s init hook and hands each server its environment and a read implementation that streams files from client/.

originFor is the origin SvelteKit compares against for CSRF: baked in at build time from paths.origin, else guessed from the headers — the guess that goes wrong behind a proxy, and why the first exists. There used to be an ORIGIN environment variable between the two; adapter-node 6 removed it and this adapter follows, because an origin that could differ between the build and the process is exactly what static: true on PUBLIC_ORIGIN rules out (ch. 36). getRequest is synchronous in 3.0 — the body becomes a stream, nothing is read yet — so there is no await on it. respond passes platform, which becomes event.platform in the app: the adapter’s name, which function answered, when the process started.

Why applyReroute

The catch-all has no routes. If its reroute hook produced a different path, the response carries x-sveltekit-rerouted-url, and applyReroute(response, next) calls next with that URL; otherwise it returns the response untouched — a 404, or /_app/env.js, which every server can answer. The rerouted request is a *new* request to the owning function, so event.url there is the rerouted URL. That is the same trade every multi-function platform makes, and it is why the reroute hook is documented as not changing event.url: within one function it does not; across two, the second never saw the original.

Two things bit while building this, both about the catch-all having no routes. SvelteKit’s in-process same-origin fetch in a route-less server falls through to a *real* fetch, so PUBLIC_ORIGIN must match the port the server is actually on — the end-to-end config sets both. And handleFetch has to use globalThis.fetch when event.platform.entry is router (ch. 26), or the resolver call answers itself with a 404.

The process is one HTTP server and a shutdown that finishes the requests it has. closeIdleConnections matters: keep-alive sockets with nothing on them would otherwise hold the process open until the platform’s timeout, which is the slow, ugly kind of shutdown that looks like a hang.

Checkpoint

  • You can list the five things every adapter does and the two that only this one does.
  • You can say why the third server has no routes and what would break if it had one, and why the three cannot share a bundle.
  • You can trace /@ostinato/four-on-the-floor from the socket to the pages function.
